The chapter house takes its name from the custom of reading a chapter of the monastic rule, or of a martyrology, at a daily assembly of the community. Over time the room became the main place for meetings of the chapter, the body of canons or monks responsible for the church. Business discussed there included the administration of property, the election of officers, the admission of new members and the correction of faults among the brethren. Important individuals, such as abbots, bishops and sometimes lay patrons, might be buried within the chapter house.

Chapter houses were usually entered from the east range of the cloister, often through a doorway flanked by windows opening onto the walk. Inside, stone benches commonly ran around the walls, with a seat of higher status for the presiding dignitary. The arrangement encouraged a sense of equality among members while still marking the order of authority.

Two main plans were used. Many houses had a rectangular room, which could be covered by a timber ceiling or a stone vault supported on a central row of columns. In England, however, a polygonal plan, usually octagonal, became a distinctive feature of secular and monastic cathedrals alike. Examples at Lincoln, Salisbury, Wells and Westminster Abbey show a central pier or clustered shafts from which ribs spread outward like the branches of a tree. Large windows lit the interior, and the walls could be richly adorned with sculpture, painted decoration and floor tiles.

Regional Variations

Continental examples tend to follow different conventions. In France and Germany many chapter houses were simpler rectangular rooms, and the cathedral chapter sometimes met in a sacristy or an adjoining hall instead. Where cathedrals were served by secular canons rather than monks, a full cloister was less essential, but it was still frequently built, as at Salisbury, to provide a processional route and a setting for burial. The survival of these spaces varies greatly, since many were altered, converted or demolished after the Reformation and later upheavals.

Crypts and Undercrofts

Origins and Function

The crypt, a vaulted chamber lying wholly or partly beneath the floor of a church, is among the oldest architectural elements of the medieval cathedral. Its origins lie in the early Christian veneration of martyrs, whose tombs were visited by pilgrims and whose relics were gathered beneath altars. As churches were built over the graves of saints, or as relics were translated into new buildings, a subterranean space was often provided to house the remains and to allow the faithful to approach them. In Rome, the arrangement associated with the tomb of Saint Peter influenced later designs, in which a semicircular or ring-shaped passage allowed pilgrims to move past the burial place without disturbing the liturgy celebrated above.

The terms crypt and undercroft are not always used consistently. Crypt generally refers to a space with a primarily sacred or funerary purpose, while undercroft may describe any vaulted substructure, including those used for storage, as meeting rooms, or as chapels in their own right. Some undercrofts exist chiefly because the ground sloped and the builders needed to level a platform for the main floor above.

Early Medieval Developments

In the Carolingian and Ottonian periods, crypts became increasingly elaborate. The ring crypt, with a corridor curving around a central chamber, gave way in many regions to the hall crypt, a broad space divided by columns into several aisles and covered by small vaults. Hall crypts could extend beneath the entire eastern arm of a church, and their plan often mirrored that of the choir above. Examples in the German lands, northern Italy, and England show the form's wide reach.

The crypt at Canterbury, begun in the eleventh century and later enlarged, is among the largest in England and is known for its carved capitals. Speyer Cathedral, begun in the early eleventh century, contains an extensive hall crypt that served as a burial place for emperors. In Italy, the crypt of San Marco in Venice and that of Modena Cathedral demonstrate the regional variety of the type.

Romanesque Elaboration

During the Romanesque period, the crypt was frequently raised so that its floor lay only partly below ground level. This allowed windows to light the interior and permitted the choir above to be elevated, creating a platform on which the high altar stood in view of the congregation. Stairs on either side of the choir led down to the crypt or up to the sanctuary. Such arrangements are visible at Durham, Worcester, and San Zeno in Verona.

Crypt vaulting often served as a testing ground for construction techniques. Groin vaults and early rib vaults were employed in these lower spaces before being used on a larger scale in the main church, and the heavy piers and thick walls required to support the structure above gave crypts their characteristic solidity.

Gothic Changes

With the rise of Gothic architecture, the crypt declined in importance in many regions. Larger windows, taller choirs, and new devotional practices drew attention toward the upper church. Relics were increasingly displayed in elaborate shrines placed behind or near the high altar, where they could be seen by pilgrims. Even so, several Gothic cathedrals retained or incorporated major crypts. Chartres Cathedral possesses one of the longest in France, formed in part from earlier structures and arranged with chapels around its ambulatory. Bourges Cathedral has a lower church that compensated for the slope of the site and supported the choir above.

Later Uses

Over time, crypts and undercrofts acquired further purposes. They accommodated burials of bishops, canons, and benefactors, and in some cases served as parish chapels, treasuries, or chapter spaces. Some were sealed or forgotten after the Reformation or changes in liturgical practice, and were rediscovered during later restoration or archaeological work. These spaces often preserve fragments of earlier buildings, making them important sources for understanding the development of a cathedral site.

Ribbed Vaulting

Ribbed vaulting is a method of roof construction in which a framework of projecting arched members, known as ribs, supports the thinner masonry panels that fill the spaces between them. It became one of the defining structural and visual features of medieval cathedrals, and its development is closely tied to the broader transition from Romanesque to Gothic building in northern Europe.

Antecedents

Vaulting in stone was well established before the Gothic period. Romanesque builders commonly used the barrel vault, a continuous semicircular tunnel of masonry, and the groin vault, formed where two barrel vaults intersect at right angles. Both types were heavy and exerted continuous outward thrust along the walls that carried them. Walls therefore had to be thick, and windows were kept small. Groin vaults also presented practical difficulties, since the sharp lines of intersection, or groins, were hard to cut accurately and were structurally vulnerable.

Ribs were used in some regions before the twelfth century, including in parts of Lombardy, Normandy and England. The cathedral of Durham, begun in the 1090s, is often cited as an early and ambitious example of ribbed vaults applied to a large church. In these early cases ribs may have served partly as a guide for construction and partly as reinforcement along the groins, and scholars continue to debate how far they were regarded as structural in the modern sense.

Structure and Construction

In a mature ribbed vault, the ribs are built first, usually over temporary timber supports called centering. The lighter infilling panels, called webs or severies, are then laid between them. Because the ribs carry much of the load to the supports, the webs can be made thin, which reduces the total weight of the roof. Builders could also set out the ribs from stone cut to a limited number of templates, which simplified the work of the masons and allowed a degree of standardisation.

The load of a vault is gathered at points rather than along entire walls. Clusters of slender shafts running down the piers receive the ribs and carry the weight to the ground. This concentration of forces made it possible to open the walls between the piers with large windows, a change that shaped the interior appearance of Gothic churches.

The Pointed Arch and the Quadripartite Vault

Ribbed vaulting was combined with the pointed arch, which directs thrust more steeply downward than a round arch and which can be adapted to spans of differing width. With round arches, diagonal ribs across a rectangular bay rise higher than the transverse ribs, producing a domed, uneven crown. Pointed arches allowed builders to bring the crowns of all the ribs to a similar height, giving a more level vault over bays of varied proportions.

The commonest early Gothic form was the quadripartite vault, in which two diagonal ribs cross at the centre of a bay and divide it into four webs. A related form, the sexpartite vault, added a transverse rib across the middle of a bay so that the vault was divided into six sections. It was used in several important churches of the late twelfth century, including Notre-Dame in Paris and the cathedral of Laon, but was gradually displaced by the simpler quadripartite arrangement.

Flying Buttresses

Although ribbed vaults were lighter than their predecessors, they still pushed outward at the level of the springing. In tall churches this thrust was carried across the aisle roofs by flying buttresses, half-arches that rise to meet the upper wall and pass the force to massive external piers. The vault, the pier and the buttress thus formed a connected system.

Decorative Elaboration

From the thirteenth century, ribs increasingly acquired a decorative role. Additional ribs, called tiercerons and liernes, were added to the basic pattern, creating star-shaped and net-like designs. English builders were especially inventive, developing the fan vault, in which ribs of equal curvature spread from a support like the ribs of a fan, as seen in the late medieval cloisters of Gloucester. In these works the ribs often exceeded structural necessity and became a form of ornament in their own right.

Flying Buttresses and Structural Equilibrium

The flying buttress is among the most recognizable structural devices of Gothic architecture. It is an inclined masonry member, usually carried on an arch or a half-arch, that spans the aisles and chapels of a church and transmits lateral forces from the upper walls and vaults of the nave or choir to a massive pier standing outside the building. Its development allowed medieval builders to raise stone vaults to great heights while opening the walls beneath them to large areas of glass.

Forces in a Stone Vault

A stone vault is heavy, and it does not simply press downward. Because of the curved geometry of ribbed vaults, each bay pushes outward at the level of its springing, the point where the vault begins to rise from the wall. Wind acting on the large timber roof above the vault adds a further sideways load. If the supporting walls were thin and unbraced, these thrusts would tend to spread the walls apart and eventually cause cracking, leaning, or collapse.

Earlier Romanesque builders usually answered this problem with thick walls, small windows, and aisle vaults or galleries that stood against the main wall and helped to resist its movement. These solutions were effective but limited the height and the amount of light the interior could receive.

Principle of Equilibrium

Masonry structures remain stable when the line of thrust, the path along which the combined forces pass through the stone, stays within the thickness of the structural members. Stone resists compression well but tolerates very little tension, so a well-designed Gothic building is one in which the loads are kept in compression throughout.

The flying buttress contributes to this condition by intercepting the outward thrust near the level of the vault springing and carrying it across the roofs of the aisles. At the outer pier, the horizontal force combines with the weight of the pier itself, and the resulting line is directed steeply into the foundations. Pinnacles placed on top of the piers were not merely decorative. Their added weight helped to steer the line of thrust more nearly vertical and so increased the stability of the pier.

Development

Early forms of external bracing appear in the twelfth century, and historians continue to debate the sequence and the places in which the system was first used. Some buttresses were initially hidden beneath aisle roofs, where they functioned as concealed props. The decision to expose them and to design them as part of the elevation seems to have occurred in the later twelfth century in the Île-de-France. The cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris is often cited in this context, though its buttresses were substantially rebuilt and altered in later periods, which complicates any account of the original arrangement.

By the early thirteenth century, buildings such as Chartres, Reims, and Amiens used elaborate systems with more than one tier of arches. Upper arches resisted wind pressure on the roof, while lower arches received the thrust of the vaults. Later builders refined the profiles, thinned the arches, and added tracery and sculpture, so that the structural frame became a major element of the exterior appearance.

Consequences for Design

Once the walls no longer needed to bear lateral loads alone, they could be reduced to slender supports between wide windows. This change is closely tied to the growth of stained glass as a principal art of the cathedral. It also encouraged the division of the elevation into clearly articulated levels and the pursuit of ever greater vertical proportions.

The system also carried risks. Builders worked largely from accumulated practical knowledge and geometric rules rather than from calculation of forces. The partial collapse of the vaults at Beauvais in the thirteenth century, and again in the sixteenth, shows the consequences of pushing height beyond the limits of the materials and of inadequate maintenance. Regular repair of buttresses, mortar joints, and drainage remains essential to the survival of these buildings.

Elevations: Arcade, Triforium, and Clerestory

The elevation of a cathedral is the vertical arrangement of the walls that enclose the nave, choir, and transepts. In many medieval churches these walls are divided into horizontal zones, each with a distinct structural and visual role. The most common divisions are the arcade at the lowest level, the triforium or gallery above it, and the clerestory at the top. The way these zones were proportioned and combined is one of the principal means by which historians distinguish regional traditions and successive stylistic phases.

Arcade

The arcade is the row of arches that separates the central vessel of the church from the aisles. It rests on piers or columns, which carry the weight of the upper walls and, in vaulted buildings, the thrust of the vault. In Romanesque churches the arcade was usually composed of round arches supported by massive piers, often cylindrical or compound in section. Durham Cathedral, begun in the late eleventh century, alternates heavy cylindrical piers with clustered piers, giving a rhythmic pattern to the nave.

Gothic builders generally raised the height of the arcade and made the arches pointed, while reducing the apparent bulk of the supports. Compound piers, formed of a central core surrounded by attached shafts, allowed vertical lines to rise from the floor toward the vault, linking the lower zones to the ribs above. At Chartres, begun after the fire of 1194, the arcade is tall and sturdy, and it supports an elevation that was notably simplified in comparison with earlier Gothic designs.

Triforium and Gallery

Above the arcade, many churches contain a middle storey. Two forms are usually distinguished. A gallery, or tribune, is a true upper storey that opens onto the nave and extends over the aisle vault or roof, creating a usable space. A triforium, by contrast, is a narrow passage or blind arcade within the thickness of the wall, usually lying behind the aisle roof and generally not intended for regular use. The terminology is not applied uniformly, and some writers use "triforium" for both.

Early Gothic cathedrals such as Noyon, Laon, and Notre-Dame in Paris adopted a four-part elevation consisting of an arcade, a gallery, a small circular or ornamental opening level, and a clerestory. This arrangement gave great height but produced a complex wall surface. The gallery also helped to buttress the main vessel against the outward pressure of the vault.

The three-part elevation, which omitted the gallery, became standard in the High Gothic period. Chartres, Reims, and Amiens used an arcade, a relatively shallow triforium, and a large clerestory. Reducing the middle zone made it possible to enlarge the windows above. English builders developed their own variations, and the triforium in cathedrals such as Lincoln and Salisbury is often a richly moulded arcade with a strong horizontal emphasis, in contrast to the vertical stress favoured in France.

Clerestory

The clerestory is the uppermost zone of the wall, pierced by windows that admit light directly into the central vessel. Because it rises above the aisle roofs, it is able to carry glazing even when the lower zones are relatively dark. In Romanesque buildings the clerestory windows were generally small, since the wall still had to bear considerable load. The development of the rib vault and the flying buttress shifted the support of the vault to external structures, and the wall could be opened more freely.

In the later twelfth and thirteenth centuries the clerestory grew in height and in the size of its windows. At Chartres the windows are tall lancets, often paired and surmounted by a circular opening. In the Rayonnant style, exemplified by the choir of Beauvais and the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, tracery allowed the window area to expand until it occupied nearly the whole bay. Some late buildings merged the triforium with the clerestory by glazing it, so that the wall was reduced to a skeleton of slender mullions and shafts.

Significance

The balance among these zones reflects changing priorities. Early designs emphasised mass and solidity, whereas later ones stressed height, light, and a continuous upward movement of the eye. Regional preferences nevertheless persisted, and variations in elevation remain a central subject in the study of cathedral architecture.

Piers, Columns, and Capitals

The vertical supports of a medieval cathedral carry the weight of vaults, roofs, and upper walls down to the foundations, and their form changed considerably between the early Middle Ages and the late Gothic period. In architectural terminology, a pier is a massive vertical support, usually of masonry, while a column is a slender, cylindrical support, often built of stacked drums or cut from a single block. Medieval builders used both, and the choice between them reflects structural needs, regional tradition, and aesthetic preference.

Romanesque Supports

In Romanesque cathedrals, built mainly between the tenth and twelfth centuries, the nave arcade was commonly carried on heavy piers of rectangular or compound section. Compound piers had half-columns, known as shafts or responds, attached to their faces. These shafts rose through the elevation to meet the arches and ribs of the vault, visually and structurally linking the arcade with the roof. Some churches alternated stout piers with lighter supports along the nave. Sant'Ambrogio in Milan and several Norman buildings in England and Normandy show such alternation, which often corresponded to the bays of a vault that spanned two arcade openings.

Large cylindrical piers also appear in Romanesque work. At Durham Cathedral, begun in 1093, massive round piers incised with spiral, lozenge, and zigzag patterns alternate with compound piers. The incised decoration emphasizes the weight of the masonry rather than concealing it.

Gothic Developments

Early Gothic builders retained the cylindrical pier in many churches, as at Notre-Dame in Paris, where a round column topped by a capital carries the nave arcade. During the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, however, the compound pier became increasingly elaborate. At Chartres, the nave piers alternate between round and octagonal cores, each surrounded by four attached shafts. This arrangement is sometimes called a cantonned pier. The shafts on the side facing the nave continue upward to support the vault ribs, drawing the eye toward the ceiling.

In the later Gothic period, piers became more slender and more finely articulated. Clusters of thin shafts, separated by deep hollows, produced a bundled appearance often called a clustered pier. In some English cathedrals, such as Salisbury, shafts of dark Purbeck marble were set against a lighter limestone core, giving a contrast of color as well as form. In the Decorated and Perpendicular styles, and in the Flamboyant style in France, the distinction between pier and arch could diminish. Mouldings ran continuously from the floor into the arches without any intervening capital, creating an uninterrupted vertical sweep.

Capitals

The capital is the member that crowns a column or pier and mediates between the support and the load above it. Its form generally broadens upward, spreading the load over a wider area. Above it often sits an abacus, a flat slab that receives the arch or vault rib.

Romanesque capitals took several forms. The cushion capital, a block with its lower corners rounded off, was common in Germany and England. Others were carved with foliage, animals, and human figures. Narrative capitals, such as those at Vézelay and Autun in Burgundy, depict biblical scenes, saints' lives, and moral subjects, and they offered sculptors a field for invention within the structural frame.

Early Gothic capitals often retained a stylized foliage derived from the classical Corinthian type, with tightly curled leaves known as crockets. A distinctive form of the later twelfth century is the water-leaf capital. During the thirteenth century, sculptors turned to naturalistic leaves modeled on local plants, such as oak, maple, and vine. The capitals of the chapter house at Southwell Minster are often cited as an example. In the later Middle Ages, capitals became smaller and shallower, and in many buildings they were omitted altogether.

Materials and Construction

Piers were typically built with a core of rubble and mortar faced in cut stone. Columns made of drums required careful bedding to carry heavy loads without failure. Settlement, overloading, and the thrust of vaults sometimes caused piers to lean or crack, and several cathedrals required later reinforcement or rebuilding of their supports.

Window Tracery

Window tracery is the ornamental stonework that divides the upper part of a Gothic window into smaller openings and supports the glass set within it. It developed in northern France in the early thirteenth century and became one of the most recognisable features of medieval cathedral design. Tracery served both structural and decorative purposes: it stiffened large openings against wind pressure, held panes of glass and iron support bars in place, and gave each window a distinctive pattern that could be read as part of the wider architectural composition.

Origins: Plate Tracery

The earliest Gothic windows were simple lancets, tall narrow openings with pointed heads. When two or more lancets were grouped under a single arch, the wall surface between them and the arch above was often pierced with a circular or foil-shaped opening. This arrangement is known as plate tracery, because the openings appear to be cut through a flat plate of masonry. Examples survive at Chartres Cathedral, where the clerestory windows combine paired lancets with a large circle above them. In plate tracery the solid stone remains the dominant element, and the openings read as holes in a wall.

Bar Tracery

The decisive change came in the 1210s and 1220s, most famously in the work at Reims Cathedral. Masons began to build the divisions of the window from slender stone bars, called mullions below and tracery bars above, so that the stone became a thin framework rather than a perforated surface. Bar tracery allowed much larger areas of glass, and its patterns could be laid out geometrically with compass and straightedge. Templates of wood or parchment were prepared for each shaped stone, and masons' lodges kept and exchanged drawings, which helped the style spread rapidly across Europe. The Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, consecrated in 1248, shows how far the technique could reduce the visible masonry in favour of glass.

Geometric and Rayonnant Styles

In the mid-thirteenth century, designs were based largely on circles, trefoils, quatrefoils and other foiled shapes combined within a pointed arch. In England this phase is often called Geometric, and in France the more elaborate developments are grouped under the term Rayonnant, from the radiating spokes of the great rose windows. The transept rose windows of Notre-Dame in Paris, begun in the mid-thirteenth century, and the west rose of Strasbourg are frequently cited examples. Rayonnant designers also applied tracery to wall surfaces, to gables and to screens, so that the pattern of the windows seemed to continue across the whole building.

Curvilinear and Flamboyant Forms

From the late thirteenth century, tracery moved away from strict geometry. English designers of the Decorated style developed flowing, ogee-curved bars, with pointed oval shapes known as mouchettes and daggers. At Exeter and Lincoln, and in the east window of Carlisle, the bars curve and branch in free patterns. In France and Spain a related development produced Flamboyant tracery, named for its flame-like shapes, seen in the west front of Rouen Cathedral and in many later churches. Central European builders, including those in the Parler family, adapted these forms in regional ways, and some designs incorporated net-like or looping patterns that no longer resembled their geometric ancestors.

Perpendicular Tracery

In England from the mid-fourteenth century, a distinct style emerged in which vertical mullions ran uninterrupted to the head of the window and were crossed by horizontal transoms. The resulting grid of panels, called Perpendicular, suited very large windows and could be repeated across an entire wall. The east window of Gloucester Cathedral, one of the largest of its age, is a leading example. The style also lent itself to standardised, repeatable stone parts, and it remained in use well into the sixteenth century.

Materials and Construction

Tracery was normally carved from fine-grained stone that could be cut into thin sections. Each bar was typically reinforced by horizontal and vertical iron rods set into the masonry, to which the glass panels were attached. Over time, corrosion of these rods and the effects of weather have required repair or replacement in many cathedrals. Because tracery is exposed and relatively slender, it is among the elements most often restored, and some surviving windows combine medieval stone with later replacements.

Stained Glass: Materials and Techniques

The stained glass of medieval cathedrals was produced from a small number of raw materials, worked through a sequence of specialised processes that changed little between the twelfth century and the close of the Middle Ages. The best-known account of these methods is the treatise of the monk Theophilus, written in the early twelfth century and usually titled On Divers Arts, which describes glassmaking, painting and assembly in practical detail.

Raw Materials and Glassmaking

Medieval window glass was made chiefly from sand, which supplied silica, combined with an alkaline flux. In northern Europe the flux was usually potash obtained from the ashes of beech or other forest wood, producing what modern scholars call forest glass. In the Mediterranean world, soda-rich ash from coastal plants was more common. Forest glass was relatively unstable in damp conditions, and this chemical weakness explains why many northern windows have suffered surface corrosion and pitting over the centuries.

Colour was obtained by adding metallic oxides to the molten batch. Copper could yield green or, under particular conditions, red; cobalt produced deep blue; manganese gave purple and could also be used to decolourise the melt; and iron contributed yellowish and brownish tones. Ruby glass was typically made as a thin layer of colour over clear glass, a technique known as flashing, because the pigment was so intense that a full thickness of red glass would appear almost black.

Sheets were formed mainly by two methods. In the cylinder or muff method, a glassblower shaped a long hollow cylinder, cut it along its length and flattened it into a sheet. In the crown method, a blown bubble was opened and spun into a disc, which left characteristic curved lines and a thickened centre. Both methods produced glass of uneven thickness, and this irregularity contributes to the lively, variable transmission of light seen in surviving windows.

Design, Cutting and Painting

The process began with a full-size drawing of the intended panel, often on a whitened table or board. This drawing established the figures, the colours and the positions of the lead lines. Pieces of coloured glass were then cut to match the design. Early glaziers heated the glass and traced the shape with a hot iron to induce a controlled crack, and they refined edges with a tool known as a grozing iron. The use of a diamond for cutting did not become established until the end of the period.

Details such as faces, hair, drapery folds and inscriptions were painted onto the glass with a dark pigment made from ground iron or copper oxide, powdered glass and a liquid binder such as wine or urine mixed with gum. The painter could apply the paint as lines, as a flat wash, or as a layer that was partly removed with a stylus or brush to create highlights and modelling. The painted glass was then fired in a kiln so that the pigment fused permanently to the surface.

From the early fourteenth century, silver stain became an important innovation. A compound of silver was applied to the glass and fired, producing tones from pale lemon to deep orange-gold. It allowed a single piece of glass to carry more than one colour, so that, for example, a figure's yellow hair or crown could be painted on a piece of white glass without a separate lead join.

Assembly and Installation

The fired pieces were assembled into panels using H-sectioned strips of lead, called cames, which were soldered at their joints. The panel was made weatherproof by pressing a putty-like cement into the spaces between glass and lead. Completed panels were fixed within the stone tracery or iron armatures of the window, with horizontal saddle bars and ties supporting the weight and resisting wind pressure.

This construction meant that the lead network was both structural and visual. Glaziers used the dark lines of the cames as part of the composition, outlining forms in the way that painted contours did, and the window's iron framework often shaped the arrangement of its narrative medallions and geometric fields.

Stained Glass: Iconography and Narrative Cycles

Stained glass was among the principal vehicles of religious instruction and devotion in medieval cathedrals. As Gothic builders reduced the area of solid wall in favour of large traceried openings, windows became the main surfaces on which sacred imagery was displayed. The glass transmitted coloured light into the interior, and this light was often interpreted by contemporary writers in theological terms. Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis, writing in the middle of the twelfth century, described the luminous quality of the new choir as a means of lifting the mind from the material to the immaterial, a view that influenced later commentary on the subject.

Typological Programmes

One of the most distinctive iconographic schemes in medieval glazing is typology, in which episodes from the Old Testament are paired with events from the life of Christ that were understood to fulfil them. Early examples appear at Saint-Denis and at Canterbury Cathedral, where the surviving panels from the choir clerestory and the aisles show Old Testament figures placed alongside Gospel scenes. A common pairing sets the sacrifice of Isaac against the Crucifixion, or Jonah emerging from the fish against the Resurrection. Such arrangements presumed a viewer, probably a cleric or a well-instructed visitor, who could recognise the correspondences, and they were often supported by explanatory inscriptions.

Narrative Cycles

Many windows present a continuous story in a sequence of small panels, set within geometric frames of iron and lead. The panels are usually read from bottom to top and from left to right, although the order varies between buildings. Cycles drawn from the Gospels, such as the Infancy and Passion of Christ, were widely used. Cycles devoted to the Virgin Mary became especially prominent in cathedrals dedicated to her, and the lives of saints formed another large category. At Chartres, which preserves an unusually complete body of glass from the early thirteenth century, windows illustrate the lives of Saint Nicholas, Saint Thomas the Apostle, and many others, alongside the parable of the Good Samaritan and the story of the Prodigal Son.

Chartres and the Great Lancets

The west façade of Chartres contains a window of the Tree of Jesse, which presents the genealogy of Christ as a vine growing from the sleeping figure of Jesse. The same theme appears at Saint-Denis, Canterbury, and York, and it remained common in later centuries. At Chartres, the large lancets beneath the north rose depict Saint Anne, with figures of Old Testament kings and prophets, while the south transept contains figures of the four evangelists seated on the shoulders of the prophets, an image often cited as an expression of the relationship between the two Testaments.

Rose Windows and Cosmic Order

Rose windows, set in the end walls of transepts and in west façades, tended to carry imagery of universal scope. Common subjects include the Last Judgement, the Virgin and Child surrounded by angels and prophets, and the ordering of time through the months and signs of the zodiac. The radial structure of the rose, with its repeating compartments around a central image, suited themes of hierarchy and completeness. The rose windows of Notre-Dame in Paris, Lausanne, and Strasbourg show differing approaches to this format.

Donors, Guilds, and Everyday Life

Many cathedral windows include images of the people who paid for them. Donor portraits, coats of arms, and inscriptions record royal, noble, and ecclesiastical patrons. At Chartres and Bourges, lower panels frequently depict trades such as bakers, butchers, drapers, and shoemakers, usually understood as the guilds that contributed to the glazing. These scenes provide valuable evidence for medieval commerce and craft practice, though scholars continue to debate whether every such panel should be read as a signature of donation.

Later Developments

From the fourteenth century, the use of silver stain allowed yellow tones to be applied to white glass, and figures were increasingly set beneath architectural canopies. Larger areas of lighter glass became usual, and the narrative panel gradually gave way to single standing figures or to large pictorial compositions. Yet the earlier cycles continued to shape iconographic conventions across Europe, and their survival, often through restoration and removal during wartime, remains central to the study of medieval art.

Rose Windows

The rose window is a large circular window, usually filled with stained glass and divided by stone tracery that radiates from a central point. It is among the most recognisable features of Gothic architecture, and it developed gradually from simpler circular openings found in earlier Romanesque churches. These earlier openings, sometimes called oculi or wheel windows, were generally small and pierced through thick masonry walls. Their spokes resembled those of a cart wheel, and the term "wheel window" is still applied to examples in which the divisions are straight and radiate directly from the hub.

Origins and Development

Circular windows appeared in the churches of Italy, France, Germany and England during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Some of the best-known Romanesque examples, such as those at San Zeno in Verona, were carved in stone and carried symbolic meaning related to the wheel of fortune. The shift to the fully developed rose came in the second half of the twelfth century in northern France, where builders began to exploit the structural possibilities of the pointed arch, the rib vault and the flying buttress. As walls became more skeletal and less load-bearing, larger openings could be cut into them, and the circular form was enlarged to fill the entire gable of a west front or the end wall of a transept.

Early Gothic roses, such as those associated with the cathedrals of Chartres, Laon and Paris, relied on a relatively simple arrangement of columns and small arches radiating from the centre. Over time, masons developed bar tracery, in which thin, moulded stone bars were cut and assembled into intricate patterns. This technique permitted much larger windows with far more delicate divisions and allowed the glass to dominate the design.

Tracery Styles

Rose windows are often classified by the character of their tracery. The Rayonnant style, which flourished in France from the middle of the thirteenth century, is named for the radiating lines of its designs. The great transept roses of Notre-Dame de Paris and the west rose of Reims Cathedral show the increasing lightness and geometric refinement of this period. In the later Flamboyant style, curving, flame-like forms replaced the more regular geometry. The west rose of Rouen and the transept windows of Sainte-Chapelle in Paris illustrate the intricate curvilinear patterns that became popular in the fifteenth century and later.

English builders favoured different arrangements. Some English roses, such as the so-called Bishop's Eye and Dean's Eye at Lincoln Cathedral, are notable for their asymmetrical or looser designs. In general, English cathedrals tended to rely less on a single monumental rose on the west front and more on large traceried windows of other shapes.

Symbolism and Iconography

The circular shape carried rich associations in medieval thought. It was linked to eternity, to the completeness of divine order, and to the cosmos. Many roses were dedicated to the Virgin Mary, and the name itself may refer to the rose as a Marian symbol, although the origin of the term is debated. Common subjects included the Last Judgement, the Virgin and Child surrounded by prophets and kings, scenes from the Apocalypse, and the signs of the zodiac and labours of the months. Christ or the Virgin was commonly placed at the centre, with ranks of figures arranged in concentric rings.

Placement and Function

Roses were most often located on the west façade above the main portal, and in the north and south arms of the transept. Their position affected both appearance and meaning. A west rose caught the light of the setting sun, while a north rose received indirect light and often used deeper blues. Within the interior, the windows acted as luminous focal points and helped to create the coloured light that was central to the Gothic idea of the church as an image of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Conservation

Many medieval roses have survived with a significant proportion of their original glass, but others have been damaged by war, weather, fire and earlier restoration. Conservation work today typically involves stabilising the stone tracery, cleaning and repairing the glass, and adding protective glazing on the exterior.

Portal Sculpture and Tympana

The portals of medieval cathedrals were among the most important sites for figural sculpture in Europe. Positioned at the threshold between the secular world and the sacred interior, they served as both entrances and visual statements of theology, and they were often the first part of the building that a visitor encountered. The sculptural programs of the great doorways developed from modest Romanesque beginnings into elaborate ensembles that covered the jambs, lintels, archivolts and trumeaux of the western façade and the transept ends.

Romanesque Origins

In the Romanesque period, sculpture became closely integrated with the architecture of the doorway. The semicircular tympanum, the field of stone enclosed by the lintel and the arch above it, became the principal surface for a single dominant image. At Autun, the Last Judgment tympanum carries the signature of the sculptor Gislebertus and dates to the second quarter of the twelfth century. At Vézelay, the narthex portal depicts the mission of the apostles, while at Moissac the south portal presents the vision of the Apocalypse, with Christ enthroned and surrounded by the elders. These works favoured elongated figures, strong linear rhythms and a hierarchical scale in which the most important figure was the largest. The imagery was frequently didactic, intended to remind the faithful of judgment and salvation.

The Gothic Portal at Saint-Denis and Chartres

The development of the Gothic portal is commonly traced to the abbey church of Saint-Denis, where the west façade was completed under Abbot Suger in the 1140s. The portals there introduced column statues on the jambs, a feature that would shape cathedral sculpture for generations. Although much of the original work has been damaged or replaced, its influence is evident at Chartres. The Royal Portal of Chartres Cathedral, carved in the middle of the twelfth century, places elongated standing figures of kings and queens against the columns flanking the doors. These figures are fused with the architecture, yet their faces show a new attention to individual character. The central tympanum shows Christ in majesty, with the symbols of the four evangelists, while the flanking portals depict the Ascension and the Virgin and Child.

Structure of a Gothic Portal

A typical Gothic portal was organised into clearly distinguished zones, each with its own function in the overall program.

The tympanum held the principal narrative or devotional scene, often divided into horizontal registers.

The lintel, below the tympanum, commonly carried a continuing sequence such as the resurrection of the dead or scenes from a saint's life.

The archivolts, the concentric bands of carving around the tympanum, were filled with angels, prophets, elders or other figures arranged in order.

The jambs held statues of apostles, prophets, or saints, standing in for the community of the Church.

The trumeau, the central pier dividing a double doorway, frequently bore a dominant figure such as Christ, the Virgin or a local patron saint.

Gothic Naturalism and Narrative

During the thirteenth century, sculptors at Reims, Amiens, Bourges and Strasbourg moved toward greater naturalism. Figures turned their heads, shifted their weight and interacted with one another, and drapery began to follow the form of the body beneath. The Last Judgment portals at Bourges and Amiens organised the scene into clear tiers, with the archangel weighing souls, the blessed proceeding toward heaven and the damned led toward hell. The Visitation group at Reims shows a marked debt to ancient models in its drapery and poise, a feature that has prompted much scholarly discussion about the transmission of classical forms.

Iconographic Themes and Reception

Common themes included the Last Judgment, the Coronation of the Virgin, the lives of local saints and the signs of the zodiac with the labours of the months. Such programs were designed in consultation with clergy and addressed audiences of differing education. Most portals were originally painted and in some cases gilded, and traces of pigment survive on a number of examples. Weathering, iconoclasm during the Reformation and the French Revolution, and later restoration have altered many of these ensembles, so that their present appearance often differs substantially from what medieval viewers saw.

Gargoyles, Grotesques, and Misericords

The carved figures that populate the exteriors and interiors of medieval cathedrals form one of the most distinctive categories of Gothic sculpture. Although they are often discussed together, gargoyles, grotesques, and misericords differ in function, placement, and probable meaning. Each reflects the close relationship between practical construction needs and the imaginative vocabulary of medieval craftsmen.

Gargoyles

A gargoyle, in the strict sense, is a carved waterspout. Its purpose is to project rainwater from the roof gutters away from the walls, so that water does not run down the masonry and erode the mortar joints. The term derives from the Old French gargouille, related to words for the throat or gullet, and it is thought to echo the gurgling sound of water passing through the channel. Typically the water ran along a lead-lined gutter and emerged through a groove or tube cut into the length of the stone figure, then fell clear of the building from the open mouth.

Gargoyles are most often found on buttresses, parapets, and the upper stages of towers, where the greatest volume of water collects. They took the form of dragons, birds, beasts, human figures, and composite creatures. The development of the flying buttress in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries gave builders many more projecting surfaces on which to place them. Cathedrals such as Notre-Dame de Paris, Reims, and Chartres carry notable examples, though many surviving figures are later replacements, since weathering and restoration have altered the original sculptural programs. The introduction of downpipes and lead spouts in later periods reduced the practical need for gargoyles, and the form became increasingly ornamental.

Grotesques

Carved figures that do not convey water are properly called grotesques, or sometimes chimeras. They occupy similar locations on pinnacles, cornices, and ledges, and are frequently confused with gargoyles in popular usage. Because they have no drainage function, grotesques could be placed freely and given more elaborate poses, such as crouching, leaning, or gazing outward over the city. Many of the best-known figures at Notre-Dame de Paris are of this kind; the famous brooding creatures on the upper gallery were largely the work of nineteenth-century restorers, who drew on medieval precedent rather than reproducing a documented original series.

Interpretation

The meaning of these figures has long been debated. Some medieval writers, including Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth century, criticized monstrous imagery in sacred settings as a distraction. Modern scholars have proposed several explanations. One holds that the figures served an apotropaic role, warding off evil. Another sees them as symbols of the forces of sin and disorder that lay outside the sanctified space of the church. A third emphasizes the pleasure of invention and the tradition of marginal imagery, also found in illuminated manuscripts. These explanations are not mutually exclusive, and the evidence for any single intention is limited.

Misericords

Misericords are carvings of a different kind, found inside the church. They are small ledges on the underside of the hinged seats of choir stalls. When the seat was folded up, a monk or canon could lean against the ledge during the long services at which standing was required, gaining some relief while appearing to stand. The name comes from the Latin for mercy or compassion.

The carved supports beneath the ledge were hidden when the seat was down and were largely free from close clerical oversight. As a result, they display a wide range of subjects: scenes of everyday labor, animal fables, proverbs, satirical episodes, mythical beasts, and occasional biblical or moral themes. Notable sets survive in English cathedrals such as Exeter, Lincoln, Ely, and Chester, and in many continental churches. Because they were intended for modest, close-range viewing, they offer valuable evidence of medieval humor, social life, and popular imagery that more formal sculpture rarely records.

Wall Painting, Pavements, and Labyrinths

Wall Painting

Although modern visitors tend to remember medieval cathedrals as spaces of bare stone, the interiors were once extensively coloured. Masonry was often covered with a thin layer of limewash or plaster and then painted, either with figural scenes or with schemes that emphasised architectural structure. Common decorative devices included red or white lines imitating mortar joints, painted masonry patterns, and bands of foliage or geometric ornament that picked out ribs, arches, and capitals. Sculpture, including column figures and tomb effigies, was likewise painted and sometimes gilded.

Figural wall painting served didactic and devotional purposes. Subjects included the Last Judgment, often placed over a chancel arch or on a west wall where it would be seen by departing worshippers; the lives of saints; scenes from the Passion; and cycles drawn from the Old Testament. Images of Saint Christopher were frequently placed opposite the main entrance, reflecting a belief that seeing the saint protected a person from sudden death for the rest of the day. Paintings in the Romanesque tradition, such as those preserved in the Catalan Pyrenees and in parts of France, tend toward large, flat forms with strong outlines. Gothic painting gradually became more naturalistic and was influenced by developments in manuscript illumination and panel painting.

Techniques varied. True fresco, in which pigment is applied to wet plaster, was used especially in Italy. In northern Europe, painting on dry plaster, often with an organic binder, was more common, and this made the surfaces more vulnerable to flaking and damp. Many schemes were whitewashed over in later centuries, particularly after the Reformation in regions where Protestant authorities opposed religious imagery, and a number have been uncovered by modern conservation work.

Pavements

Cathedral floors were also decorated. The most common medieval flooring was stone slab, but many major churches had pavements of glazed tile, inlaid stone, or mosaic. In England and France, decorated ceramic tiles were made in workshops that supplied cathedrals, monasteries, and wealthy households. The tiles were typically impressed or inlaid with heraldic devices, animals, foliage, and geometric motifs, and were laid in repeating patterns, especially in chapter houses and around shrines.

In Italy, the tradition of mosaic and inlaid marble remained strong. The technique known as opus sectile, which uses cut pieces of coloured stone fitted together, produced elaborate geometric designs, and in some churches the Cosmati workshops of Rome and its surroundings created pavements of porphyry and marble roundels set in intricate frames. At Siena, the cathedral pavement developed into an extended programme of figural panels made by many artists over a long period, using marble inlay and incised work. Floors could therefore carry as much iconographic weight as walls and windows.

Labyrinths

A distinctive feature of some Gothic cathedrals is the labyrinth set into the nave floor. These designs, usually composed of a single winding path leading to a centre, are found in a number of northern French churches, including Chartres, Amiens, and Reims, as well as in some Italian examples. The best-known type, the Chartres pattern, is circular and divides into quadrants, with a path that turns back repeatedly before reaching the middle.

The purpose of medieval labyrinths is not fully documented. Later tradition describes them as substitutes for pilgrimage to Jerusalem, with the faithful following the path on their knees or on foot as a devotional exercise, and they are also sometimes associated with the Easter liturgy. Some surviving evidence suggests that clergy used certain labyrinths in ceremonial dances or ball games at Easter. Because documentary sources are limited and often late, scholars treat both explanations with caution. Many labyrinths were damaged or removed in the post-medieval period, when they were thought to distract from worship, and a number have since been restored or recreated.

Liturgical Furnishings: Altars, Screens, and Choir Stalls

The interior of a medieval cathedral was shaped as much by its furnishings as by its masonry. Altars, screens, and stalls organized the movement of clergy and laity, marked the boundaries between sacred and public space, and gave physical form to the hierarchy of those who worshipped there. Many of these fittings were removed or damaged during the Reformation, the French Revolution, and later restorations, so surviving examples are often fragmentary, and much of what is known comes from inventories, building accounts, and the study of the few ensembles that remain.

Altars

The high altar stood at the liturgical center of the cathedral, usually in the eastern arm of the church, and was the focus of the principal daily offices and the Mass. Early medieval altars were often simple tables of stone or wood, sometimes placed over or near the tomb or relics of a saint. From the central Middle Ages, altars were increasingly furnished with a retable, a painted or sculpted panel placed at the back or above the altar table. Retables could be made of carved and gilded wood, stone, metalwork, or painted panels, and they frequently depicted Christ, the Virgin, or the patron saint of the church. In some churches, notably in the Rhineland and the Low Countries, large winged altarpieces with hinged panels could be opened or closed according to the liturgical calendar.

Cathedrals also contained many secondary altars. These were set in side chapels, in the ambulatory, along the aisles, and against screens and piers. They were endowed by bishops, canons, guilds, and wealthy families, often to support the singing of Masses for the souls of the dead. The growth of private and commemorative Masses encouraged the multiplication of altars and chapels, and it influenced the design of radiating chapels around the east end in many Gothic churches.

Screens

Screens divided the cathedral into zones of differing access. The most prominent was the rood screen, or jubé in French, which separated the choir from the nave. It carried a gallery from which the Gospel or Epistle could be read, and it was often surmounted by a rood, a crucifix flanked by figures of the Virgin and Saint John. Rood screens were built of wood or stone, and many were richly painted and carved. Altars of the laity were often placed against their western face, so that the nave congregation could attend Mass even when the choir was closed to them.

Origins and Prehistory of Textile Making

The making of cloth is among the oldest of human technologies, yet it is also one of the least well preserved in the archaeological record. Fibres, threads and fabrics are organic and decay readily, so the earliest history of textiles must be reconstructed largely from indirect evidence: impressions left in clay, tools made of stone, bone and fired clay, depictions in art, and the rare finds that survive in unusually dry, frozen, waterlogged or salt-rich conditions.

Before Weaving

Many researchers believe that the working of plant and animal fibres began long before the appearance of woven cloth. Cordage, nets, baskets and mats require the twisting, knotting and interlacing of flexible materials, and these techniques are likely to have preceded the loom. Fragments of twisted fibre found at sites in Europe and western Asia indicate that people were making string by the Upper Palaeolithic. A well-known example is the cluster of flax fibres, some of them twisted and some dyed, recovered from Dzudzuana Cave in the Caucasus region and dated to roughly thirty thousand years ago. These finds suggest that spun and coloured fibres were already part of daily life among hunter-gatherer communities.

Further evidence comes from impressions of textiles and cords on fired clay. Fragments of figurines and pottery from Central Europe, including material from the Czech Republic dated to the Gravettian period, bear the marks of woven or netted structures. Such impressions show that techniques such as plaiting and simple weaving were known, even though the original objects have vanished. Bone needles with eyes, known from Palaeolithic sites in Eurasia, point to the sewing of skins and perhaps of other materials.

Felting and Early Fabrics

Felt is sometimes proposed as one of the earliest true fabrics, since it needs no spinning or loom; matted animal fibre can be formed through moisture, heat and pressure. Because felt is fragile, direct evidence from the earliest periods is scarce. Some of the oldest surviving examples come from the burial sites of the steppe and the Altai mountains, where frozen tombs preserved felt hangings, garments and saddle coverings from the first millennium BCE. The sophisticated decoration of these pieces implies a long preceding tradition.

Spinning, Weights and the Loom

By the Neolithic period, textile production had become a substantial activity in many regions. The spindle whorl, a small weight of stone, clay or bone that regulates the spin of a spindle, is among the most common textile-related finds on archaeological sites. Loom weights, which hold warp threads taut on an upright loom, appear in large numbers in settlements across Europe and the Near East. Their presence offers a way to trace where weaving was practised, even when no cloth survives.

Linen was the characteristic fabric of early farming societies in the Near East and Egypt, where flax was cultivated and woven into cloth of great fineness. Fragments from Neolithic sites such as Çatalhöyük in Anatolia and from caves in the Judean desert are among the earliest preserved woven pieces. In the Swiss and Alpine lake settlements, waterlogged deposits have yielded linen textiles, fishing nets and cords. Wool became prominent later, after sheep were bred for fleeces rather than only for meat and milk, a development often linked to the so-called secondary products revolution of the Bronze Age.

Independent Beginnings

Textile technology did not spread from a single centre. In East Asia, silk production from the cocoon of the domesticated silkworm developed in China, with evidence of silk fabric from Neolithic contexts. Wool and Animal Hair Fibers

Animal fibers are among the oldest raw materials used in textile production. Because they are shorn, combed, or gathered from living animals, they have supplied many communities with a renewable source of material for clothing, shelter, bedding, and trade goods. The properties of a fiber depend on the species, the breed, the part of the body from which it is taken, and the conditions in which the animal lives. Craftspeople have long learned to match each fiber to a purpose, and many regional textile traditions are closely tied to the animals raised in a given landscape.

Sheep Wool

Sheep wool is the most widely used animal fiber in traditional textile work. Its surface is covered in microscopic scales, and the fiber has a natural crimp, or waviness. These features allow wool to trap air, to resist moisture to some degree, and to bind to itself when worked with heat, moisture, and pressure, which is the basis of felting. Wool also accepts natural dyes readily, which has made it a favored fiber for dyers.

Breeds differ greatly. Fine-wool breeds, such as the merino, which developed in Spain and later spread across the world, produce soft fleece suited to garments worn against the skin. Medium wools are versatile and are used for knitting and weaving. Long-wool and coarse-wool breeds yield strong, lustrous or hardy fibers that are well suited to rugs, carpets, blankets, and outer garments. In many pastoral regions, such as the highlands of Central Asia, Anatolia, and the Atlantic islands of northern Europe, local breeds produce distinctive fleece that shapes the character of regional cloth. Some primitive breeds have a double coat, in which a soft undercoat lies beneath longer, coarser outer hairs.

Goat Fibers

Goats supply several valued fibers. Cashmere is the soft undercoat of certain goats raised in the high, cold regions of Central Asia, and it is usually gathered by combing during the spring molt. Mohair comes from the Angora goat, whose name recalls the Anatolian region where the breed is believed to have originated. Mohair is lustrous, strong, and smooth, and it takes dye with brilliance. Coarser goat hair has long been spun and woven into tent cloth, ropes, and bags by nomadic peoples of the Middle East and North Africa, where the dark, tough cloth sheds rain once the fibers swell.

Camelids

The camel family provides some of the most distinctive fibers. Domesticated camels shed a soft undercoat that is collected and spun into warm yarn, often left in its natural tan or brown shades. In the Andes, the llama and alpaca have been central to textile life for many centuries. Alpaca fiber is soft, lustrous, and available in a wide range of natural colors. Llama fiber is typically coarser and is often used for cordage, bags, and heavy cloth. The vicuña, a wild relative, produces an extremely fine fiber, and in the past its harvest was reserved for elites; today it is regulated for conservation. The guanaco is another wild camelid whose fleece has occasionally been used.

Other Animal Hairs

Many other animals contribute to textile traditions. Rabbit hair, notably from the Angora rabbit, is light and fluffy and is usually blended with other fibers. Yak hair, gathered in the Himalayan and Tibetan highlands, is used for tents, ropes, and warm cloth. Musk ox undercoat, known as qiviut, is gathered by Arctic peoples and by modern cooperatives and is valued for its softness and warmth. Horsehair has been used for stiff fabrics, braiding, and ornamental work, and dog hair has been spun in some regions, including among Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest of North America, where it was historically blended with other fibers in woven blankets.

Preparation of Fibers

Whatever the source, fibers pass through similar stages before they are made into cloth. They are shorn or combed, sorted by quality, and cleaned of dirt and natural grease. They are then opened up by carding, which aligns fibers in a loose mass, or by combing, which produces a smoother arrangement with the longer fibers kept together. Spinning with a spindle or wheel turns the prepared fiber into yarn. Fiber that is instead to be felted may be used directly after carding, without spinning.

Bast Fibers: Flax, Hemp, and Ramie

Bast fibers are strands of plant tissue found in the outer stem of certain dicotyledonous plants, lying between the bark and the woody core. Unlike cotton, which grows as a seed hair, or wool, which is shorn from animals, bast fibers must be freed from the stem through a sequence of steps before they can be spun. Flax, hemp, and ramie are the best known of these plants, and each has supported textile traditions across many regions for thousands of years.

Flax

Flax (Linum usitatissimum) yields the fiber used for linen. Archaeological finds of twisted and woven flax from sites in the Near East and in the Caucasus suggest that the plant was worked by people in prehistoric times, and linen was a central cloth in ancient Egypt, where it was used for clothing, sails, and the wrapping of the dead. Linen later became a major cloth of medieval and early modern Europe, with important centers of production in Flanders, Ireland, the Baltic lands, and parts of Russia.

Traditionally, flax is pulled up by the roots rather than cut, so that the full length of the fiber is preserved. The seeds are removed by a process called rippling. The stalks are then retted, meaning they are soaked in ponds or streams, or left on the ground to be exposed to dew, so that microorganisms break down the pectins that bind the fibers to the stem. After drying, the stalks are broken with a wooden brake, and the remaining woody fragments are scraped away with a wooden blade in a step known as scutching. Finally, the fibers are drawn through combs called hackles, which separate the long, fine line fibers from the shorter tow. Line fiber is usually spun wet on a spinning wheel or with a distaff and spindle, which produces a smooth, strong thread.

Hemp

Hemp (Cannabis sativa) was cultivated in East Asia from early times, and fragments of hemp cloth and cord are among the oldest known textile remains from China. In Europe and elsewhere it was valued for rope, sailcloth, sacking, and coarse household fabric, though finer hemp cloth was also made. In Korea, hemp cloth called sambe has long been woven for everyday garments and for mourning dress. In parts of Eastern Europe, hemp was also made into household linens and ritual cloths.

The processing of hemp follows steps similar to those used for flax, although the stalks are taller and the fiber is generally coarser. Hemp cloth tends to soften with use and washing, and it takes dye well.

Ramie

Ramie (Boehmeria nivea) is a perennial plant of the nettle family native to East Asia. Its fiber is notable for its length, strength, and natural luster. Ramie cloth has been woven in China for a very long time, and it was made in Korea and Japan as well. Korean mosi, a fine cloth woven from ramie, is produced in the Hansan region and is recognized as an intangible cultural heritage. Because ramie fibers are held in place by a gum, the stems are typically stripped by hand, and the fibers are scraped and degummed before use. Short lengths are spliced end to end, often by twisting them together with the fingers, to form a continuous yarn without a spindle. The resulting cloth is light, crisp, and cool to wear, which made it especially suitable for summer garments in warm, humid climates.

Qualities and Continuing Practice

Bast fiber cloth is generally strong, absorbent, and quick to dry, and it tends to become softer and more lustrous with age. These qualities explain its long use in clothing, bedding, and household textiles. In many regions the cultivation and preparation of these fibers declined as cotton and synthetic fibers became widely available, but handwork traditions continue among artisans, cultural organizations, and farming communities that value the plants and the skills associated with them.

Cotton Cultivation and Processing

Cotton is a soft fibre that grows in a protective capsule, called a boll, on shrubs of the genus Gossypium. It is among the most widely used natural fibres in the history of textile production. Several species were domesticated independently in different parts of the world. Old World cottons were cultivated in the Indus Valley, in parts of Africa, and later across Asia, while New World cottons were grown in the Andean region and in Mesoamerica. Archaeological finds of cotton cord and cloth in South Asia and coastal Peru show that the plant was used for textiles for thousands of years before the modern era.

Growing Conditions and Cultivation

Cotton grows best in warm climates with a long frost-free season, plentiful sunlight, and enough moisture during the growing period. It is traditionally sown in spring, once the soil has warmed. Farmers have long adapted their methods to local conditions. In river valleys, seasonal flooding or irrigation channels supplied water. In drier regions, cotton was often planted in small plots near homes, where it could be tended alongside food crops. Some traditional systems relied on rainfall alone, and others used intercropping, in which cotton shares a field with beans, millet, or other plants.

After flowering, the blossoms fade and the boll develops. When it is ripe, it splits open and reveals a mass of white fibre surrounding the seeds. Naturally coloured varieties also exist. Brown, tan, and greenish cottons were grown in the Americas and have been maintained by some weavers and growers who value them for their undyed tones.
